missing_values: `company` is missing for 94% and `agent` for 14% of bookings, so neither is used as a forecasting feature. Only 4 `children` and 488 `country` values are missing - harmless for a demand forecast.
duplicates_sensitivity: 31,994 rows (26.8%) are exact copies of another row. Dropping them lowers total room-nights to 86% of the keep-all level but the two daily series have correlation 0.942, so weekly/seasonal shape - what a forecaster learns - is unchanged. The absolute level may be understated if some copies are genuine repeat bookings (no booking ID exists to prove either way).
cancellation: 37.0% of bookings are cancelled - ignoring them would overstate demand by about a third. Cancellation climbs from 10% for last-minute bookings to 68% beyond a year of lead time, and 'Non Refund' deposits cancel at 99% (implausibly high, so it likely reflects how the source system recorded these bookings; deposit type is not used). This is why the model counts bookings 'on the books' at the origin only if not yet cancelled by then.
arrival_distribution: Arrivals span 2015-07-01 to 2017-08-31 (793 consecutive days, no gaps). Volume peaks in summer (max 448 arrivals/day) and troughs in winter; 2015 and 2017 are partial years, so the data holds only two full summers (2016, 2017) plus July-August 2015 - a key limit for learning seasonality.
weekday_pattern: Sat is the busiest night and Sun the quietest; weekend nights average -2.2% versus weekdays. The weekday pattern is modest but consistent, which is exactly what the seasonal-naive baseline exploits.
monthly_trend: Demand peaks in Jun and bottoms out in winter. Comparing Jan-Aug, 2017 averages +9.2% versus 2016 (2015 has July-December only), so there is a level shift on top of the seasonal cycle - a plain 'same as last year' rule would be biased.
room_categories: Type A holds 72% of reservations. 12.5% of guests are placed in a different type from the one reserved, and assigned types I and K never appear as reservations - so assigned type is a check-in outcome. We forecast by RESERVED type and pool the rare types B, C, H, L, P into 'Other'.
lead_time: Median lead time is 69 days but the mean is 104: a long right tail (max 737) of very early bookings. 43% of bookings are made more than 90 days ahead, which is what makes 'on-the-books' counts informative 7-14 days out.
adr: Price follows demand: mean ADR is highest in Aug (141) and lowest in Jan (72), with the Resort Hotel far more seasonal than the City Hotel. 1,959 raw rows have ADR = 0 and one has 5,400 (excluded from the chart tail); ADR is not a model feature because it is only observed with the booking, not forecastable demand.
seasonality_heatmap: Month matters more than weekday: Jun-Aug averages 1.7x Dec-Feb, while the busiest weekday in a month is on average only 17% above the quietest. Calendar features therefore set the level, and recent history + bookings on the books supply the day-level detail.
correlation: lead_time is the attribute most correlated with cancellation (r = 0.18); ADR vs month r = 0.11. These are booking-level attributes. For forecasting we correlate demand with its own history instead (see the lag features), and correlation is not used as causal evidence.
outliers: Lead time, ADR and length of stay all have long right tails. ADR 5,400 and stays of 69 nights are extreme but still plausible bookings, so they are kept; they affect room-night counts by at most a handful of rows. Hard errors (zero nights, zero guests, negative ADR) are removed instead. See reports/cleaning_report.json.
target_series: Category A carries 60% of room-nights, D 23%, E 9%; F, G and Other are small (8% together), so their daily counts are noisy and will show the largest relative error. Target = room-nights on the stay date from bookings NOT cancelled; this is booking demand, not physical occupancy.
